paragraphs: Subgraph graph neural networks offer ways to recognize graph structure that simpler architectures may miss. Yet many different designs exist, making it difficult to tell which architectural choices actually increase expressive power. This paper develops a systematic comparison for node-based subgraph GNNs using Subgraph Weisfeiler-Lehman tests, or SWL.

The central theoretical result organizes these models into six equivalence classes with strictly increasing expressiveness. Models in the same class have equivalent distinguishing power under this framework, while moving upward adds capabilities. The class called SSWL reaches the highest expressiveness within the studied family. The authors also examine concrete structural capabilities, including representing graph distances and biconnectivity.

Connections to localized WL and Folklore WL tests establish a tight upper bound and expose an inherent gap between SWL and 2-FWL. Thus, the hierarchy identifies both a strongest design target and a ceiling for the family. Experiments further show that simple architectures inspired by SSWL can substantially outperform earlier models on multiple benchmarks, connecting the theoretical organization to practical architecture design.
icml-2023-a-complete-expressiveness-hier.tldr: The paper classifies node-based subgraph GNNs into six expressiveness levels, identifying a maximal class that inspires simple, effective architectures.

paragraphs: Differentiable physics simulators allow robot policies to learn through gradients of simulated motion. Contact makes this difficult: the paper shows that complementarity-based contact systems can be stiff, causing the variance of first-order policy gradients to explode. Consequently, even an accurate contact model can produce an optimization landscape that is chaotic and nonsmooth.

Adaptive Barrier Smoothing, or ABS, softens the complementarity system through objectives smoothed by barriers. Its smoothing parameter adapts to contact conditions, reducing gradient variance while controlling the bias introduced by smoothing. This distinction matters because a more stable gradient is useful only if it still provides sufficiently faithful guidance about the underlying task.

The authors analyze the source of stiffness to justify their adaptive design, establish convergence of first-order policy gradient, and give upper bounds describing the variance–bias trade-off. They also introduce a related policy-gradient variant that learns physical parameters to fit contact dynamics efficiently. Experiments across robotic tasks support the theory and method, suggesting that adapting the simulator’s smoothness can improve the learning process.
icml-2023-adaptive-barrier-smoothing-for.tldr: Adaptive Barrier Smoothing stabilizes policy gradients through contact dynamics by reducing gradient variance while controlling smoothing bias.

paragraphs: N:M sparsity keeps at most N weights in each group of M consecutive weights, a structure that compatible sparse tensor cores can accelerate. However, making the forward computation sparse does not automatically make backpropagation efficient. Dense computations during the backward pass can therefore limit the training benefits of this sparsity pattern.

Bi-directional Masks, or Bi-Mask, uses separate masks for forward and backward propagation. This separates the sparsity requirements of the two directions so both can benefit from acceleration. Because changing the backward mask can alter gradient computation, the method also permutes weight rows efficiently. It selects a candidate permutation with many backward blocks that satisfy the N:M constraint, aiming to reduce the gradient discrepancy relative to traditional masking.

Experiments show better predictive performance than an existing approach that uses a transposable mask to accelerate the backward pass. Bi-Mask also matches or exceeds methods that do not provide backward acceleration. The contribution is therefore a way to combine efficient training computations with preserved model performance, using directional masks and weight arrangement together.
icml-2023-bi-directional-masks-for-effic.tldr: Bi-Mask uses separate forward and backward sparsity masks plus weight-row permutations to accelerate training while maintaining predictive performance.

paragraphs: Efficient attention methods aim to make transformers handle long sequences with less computation while retaining their effectiveness. The paper argues that the widely used Long Range Arena benchmark covers only part of this problem: noncausal self-attention. Its coverage leaves out causal attention and cross-attention, even though these patterns also matter in downstream applications.

The Comprehensive Attention Benchmark, or CAB, evaluates four patterns: causal and noncausal versions of both self-attention and cross-attention. It brings together seven real-world tasks from different research areas and uses eight backbone networks. This setup allows researchers to examine whether an attention method’s performance carries across both attention patterns and the architectures surrounding it.

The authors benchmark nine widely used efficient attention architectures with different design approaches. Their experiments investigate when efficient methods become advantageous over standard attention, whether performance is consistent across patterns, and what attention itself contributes. They also examine interpolation and extrapolation in long-context language modeling. CAB’s contribution is broader evaluation coverage, making efficiency claims more informative about the settings in which a method will actually be used.
icml-2023-cab-comprehensive-attention-be.tldr: CAB benchmarks efficient attention across four attention patterns, seven tasks, and eight backbones to broaden evaluation of long-sequence modeling.

paragraphs: Real-world super-resolution must reconstruct detailed images despite variation in how inputs have been degraded. Training on a broad, complex range of degradations can improve generalization, but the authors demonstrate that this comes with reduced restoration accuracy. The practical question is how to choose training degradations that fit the application without sacrificing useful robustness.

The proposed method uses a small collection of reference images to craft the training degradation distribution. It represents the degradation space in bins and uses Fréchet distance to compare degradation distributions. These components provide a basis for shaping training around the degradation variation relevant to the intended use.

The approach rests on the observation that a particular real-world application typically encounters a limited range of degradations. Within that range, the authors argue that accuracy and generalization can be balanced more effectively. Their results show substantial improvements on test images while preserving generalization capabilities in real-world applications. The finding emphasizes that choosing the training distribution is itself an important part of building a successful restoration system.
icml-2023-crafting-training-degradation-.tldr: The method tailors super-resolution training degradations using reference images to improve application-specific accuracy while preserving generalization.

paragraphs: Adversarial detection seeks to distinguish manipulated inputs from natural ones by identifying differences in their distributions. Directly comparing high-dimensional distributions is difficult. A possible alternative is the score, the gradient of log probability density with respect to an input, but the authors find that a score from one observation provides insufficient information for reliable identification.

The paper introduces expected perturbation score, or EPS. It adds different noises to an input and averages the resulting scores, gathering multiple views of the same sample. A pretrained diffusion model can estimate this statistic in practice. Under mild conditions, the authors prove that EPS is a suitable statistic for measuring discrepancies between samples.

Their detector, EPS-AD, uses an EPS-based version of maximum mean discrepancy to compare a test input with natural samples. The paper also proves a separation result: this discrepancy is larger between natural and adversarial samples than among natural samples. Extensive experiments report superior detection performance. Together, the results support probing several perturbed views as a more informative basis for detection than inspecting one score alone.
icml-2023-detecting-adversarial-data-by-.tldr: EPS-AD detects adversarial inputs by averaging scores across noisy perturbations and comparing the resulting statistic with natural samples.

paragraphs: Federated learning often involves only a subset of devices in each training round because communication bandwidth is limited. Random selection can hurt performance when devices hold differently distributed data. The authors identify imbalance among the classes represented by the selected devices’ combined data as the essential cause of this degradation.

Federated Class-balanced Sampling, or Fed-CBS, chooses participants with their collective class balance in mind. It first defines a class-imbalance measure that can be obtained in a privacy-preserving way. A computationally efficient sampling strategy then uses that measure to select devices whose grouped data are more balanced, supported by theoretical guarantees.

The distinction is that a client is evaluated as part of a group: the training round benefits from how the selected datasets complement one another. Experiments show improved test accuracy and convergence speed over existing approaches. Performance is also comparable to, or better than, involving every available client in the reported evaluations. These findings support client selection as a way to improve the statistical quality of a training round as well as manage communication.
icml-2023-fed-cbs-a-heterogeneity-aware-.tldr: Fed-CBS selects federated clients whose combined data are more class-balanced, improving accuracy and convergence in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Personalized federated learning gives each client a model suited to its own objectives. However, scarce and heterogeneous local data can make those models overfit. FedCR addresses this by encouraging clients to learn representations shared across the federation while retaining individually trained prediction heads.

During local updates, FedCR adds a regularizer that reduces disagreement between local and global conditional mutual information. The server aggregates the feature extractor, while each client customizes its predictor. The authors theoretically connect this regularization to alignment between local and global stochastic feature distributions, measured through Kullback-Leibler divergence.

FedCR models the global joint feature distribution as a product of local feature distributions. This lets clients draw on diverse information from the wider dataset without receiving other clients’ raw data. The paper also shows how noise injection through feature alignment and an ensemble of local predictors can help generalization. Benchmark experiments report consistent performance gains and better generalization behavior. The overall approach balances shared feature learning with client-specific decisions, addressing overfitting without giving up personalization.
icml-2023-fedcr-personalized-federated-l.tldr: FedCR combines shared feature learning, information-based regularization, and personalized prediction heads to improve federated generalization.

paragraphs: Intensive-care electronic health records contain numerical measurements and clinical notes collected at uneven intervals. Their timing complicates both learning from each source and combining them. This paper builds irregular timing into the representations of both modalities and into the mechanism that fuses them for medical prediction.

For numerical time series, a gate dynamically combines handcrafted imputation embeddings with learned interpolation embeddings. For clinical notes, the method treats sequences of note representations as multivariate irregular time series and applies time attention. An interleaved attention mechanism then integrates the modalities across temporal steps, carrying timing considerations into their interaction.

Across two medical prediction tasks, the proposed methods consistently outperform state-of-the-art baselines in numerical-only, note-only, and combined settings. The reported relative F1 improvements are 6.5%, 3.6%, and 4.3%, respectively. These findings support addressing irregularity throughout the modeling process, including when information sources are fused. The contribution is a coordinated treatment of uneven observation times across measurements and text, with empirical gains in each of the evaluated input configurations.
icml-2023-improving-medical-predictions-.tldr: Modeling irregular timing within numerical records, clinical notes, and their fusion improves F1 on two medical prediction tasks.

paragraphs: Object placement inserts a foreground object into a background at a location and size that produce a natural composition. Existing methods often generate placement diversity from random vectors, but those vectors are difficult for people to interpret or control. This paper introduces IOPRE, which starts from an initial placement and improves it through sequential decisions.

The reinforcement-learning agent uses an action space that adjusts position and size while preserving the foreground object’s aspect ratio. To choose actions, it combines features of the composed image with sinusoidal positional embeddings describing the foreground. This representation provides information about both visual composition and the object’s current placement.

A hybrid reward combines placement assessment with the number of adjustment steps, guiding the agent toward visually pleasing and semantically appropriate results. Experiments on the OPA dataset show state-of-the-art plausibility and diversity. The interactive value comes from making location and size explicit starting conditions for a sequence of adjustments, giving users a more interpretable entry point than a random vector.
icml-2023-interactive-object-placement-w.tldr: IOPRE uses reinforcement learning to adjust an initial object placement through interpretable position and size changes.

paragraphs: Structure-based drug design seeks molecules that bind strongly to a target protein. Generative models can produce three-dimensional molecules conditioned on protein pockets, but treating each pocket independently overlooks similarities between their smaller local environments. Similar subpockets may bind the same molecular fragment even when the full pockets have different structures.

DrugGPS uses this local commonality to support generalization to unseen pockets. Guided by biochemical priors, it learns representative subpocket prototypes and builds a global interaction graph linking them to molecular motifs. A hierarchical graph transformer encodes structure, and a motif-based generation scheme constructs three-dimensional molecules.

This organization allows the model to use relationships between local protein environments and molecular fragments across different pockets. Experiments show consistent improvements over baselines in generating realistic candidates with high affinities under challenging out-of-distribution conditions. The stated findings support subpocket-level knowledge sharing as a useful ingredient for generalizable molecular generation. The reported achievement concerns candidate generation and affinity in those evaluations, with the architecture explicitly designed around structural connections that independent pocket modeling neglects.
icml-2023-learning-subpocket-prototypes-.tldr: DrugGPS shares information through subpocket prototypes and molecular motifs to improve molecule generation for unseen protein pockets.

paragraphs: Federated training can slow down when devices finish at different times. Another bottleneck appears when the server must perform expensive aggregation, such as knowledge distillation, before devices can continue. The paper identifies the usual aggregate-then-broadcast ordering as the underlying workflow responsible for this waiting.

Its parallel federated learning framework swaps the order of aggregation and broadcasting. The resulting pipeline allows edge devices to work during server computation and the server to work during local computation. Fully asynchronous parallel operation accommodates complex aggregation and slow participants while allowing flexible device participation and scalable computation.

The authors prove that synchronous and asynchronous versions can attain convergence rates similar to conventional federated learning. Experiments report training speedups of up to 5.56 times compared with traditional federated learning. The maximum reported gain is an empirical result, while the theoretical contribution concerns convergence rates. Together, these results show how reorganizing when work occurs can improve training efficiency without requiring all participants to wait through the same sequence of local and global computations.
icml-2023-no-one-idles-efficient-heterog.tldr: Reordering server aggregation and broadcasting enables parallel federated computation, with similar theoretical convergence rates and reported speedups up to 5.56 times.

paragraphs: This paper studies how much expressive power can come from repeatedly applying the same small neural network. Although a single fixed-size ReLU network has limited capabilities on its own, composing that network with itself creates a deeper computation. The authors analyze the approximation power available through this repeated use.

They construct a model consisting of an affine input map, r applications of the same ReLU network, and an affine output map. For 1-Lipschitz continuous functions on the d-dimensional unit cube, the construction achieves approximation error of order r raised to the power −1/d. Thus, increasing the number of compositions improves the guaranteed error, with a rate that depends on input dimension.

The result also extends to general continuous functions, with error described by their modulus of continuity, which captures how their values vary with input distance. The authors connect these findings to continuous-depth networks generated by dynamical systems. Even time-independent dynamics implemented by a fixed-size ReLU network can have substantial approximation power. This is a constructive expressiveness result about what repeated computation can represent.
icml-2023-on-enhancing-expressive-power-.tldr: Repeatedly composing a single fixed-size ReLU network yields provable approximation power that increases with the number of repetitions.

paragraphs: Linear contextual bandits learn which actions yield higher rewards from contextual information. This paper studies the case where a linear model only approximates expected rewards, with bounded error ζ. It asks how that error interacts with the smallest reward gap Δ between optimal and suboptimal choices and the context dimension d.

The proposed algorithm updates its online regression using only context vectors with large uncertainty. When ζ is sufficiently small relative to Δ divided by the square root of d, up to logarithmic factors, it achieves the same gap-dependent regret bound as in the correctly specified setting: approximately d squared divided by Δ. The authors also show that SupLinUCB can achieve a gap-dependent constant regret bound without knowing Δ.

Combined with a lower bound, the results suggest a learnability threshold at the scale Δ divided by the square root of d, with logarithmic qualifications. Below this scale, efficient learning is possible; above it, the lower bound indicates an obstruction. Synthetic and real-world experiments corroborate the theory, connecting tolerance to model error with the difficulty of distinguishing action rewards.
icml-2023-on-the-interplay-between-missp.tldr: Gap-dependent learning remains possible when linear bandit misspecification is sufficiently small relative to the reward gap and context dimension.

paragraphs: Kernel ridge regression estimates a function using a kernel-defined function space and regularization. In the misspecified setting studied here, the true function belongs to a less-smooth interpolation space associated with a reproducing kernel Hilbert space. A parameter s between zero and one describes the smoothness regime under consideration.

Previous minimax-optimality results required the true function to be bounded in the L-infinity sense. In the setup described by the authors, that requirement implicitly restricts s to values above an embedding index determined by the kernel space. This leaves part of the interval between zero and one outside the reach of those results, raising the question of whether kernel ridge regression remains optimal there.

The paper proves minimax optimality throughout the full interval when the kernel space is a Sobolev RKHS. Minimax optimality concerns the best achievable worst-case statistical rate over the relevant function class. The result therefore extends the theoretical justification for kernel ridge regression into rougher-function regimes. Its stated scope is specifically Sobolev kernel spaces, for which it resolves the smoothness-range question posed in the abstract.
icml-2023-on-the-optimality-of-misspecif.tldr: For Sobolev kernel spaces, kernel ridge regression is minimax optimal across the full misspecified smoothness range s between zero and one.

paragraphs: Sparse recovery usually relates observations to unknown signals through a known sensing matrix. This paper considers an additional difficulty: the correspondence between observations and sensing rows is missing or incomplete. An unknown permutation represents that mismatch, and additive noise further complicates recovery across multiple measurements.

Earlier work on multiple measurements focused on having more samples than signal dimensions. Here, the authors investigate the substantially undersampled regime, where the number of samples is much smaller than the ambient dimension, while assuming the unknown signal matrix is sparse. They first establish lower bounds on the sample count and signal-to-noise ratio required to recover the correct permutation.

The paper then presents a simple estimator and proves that, under mild conditions, it restores the correct correspondence with high probability. Numerical experiments support the theoretical claims. The significance is that missing correspondence can be addressed even in an undersampled setting when signal sparsity is available. The guarantees remain conditional, and the specific recovery claim highlighted in the abstract is identification of the correct permutation.
icml-2023-one-step-estimator-for-permute.tldr: The paper gives recovery lower bounds and a simple estimator for identifying missing measurement correspondences in undersampled sparse recovery.

paragraphs: Second-order optimization uses curvature information to choose updates, often through an inverse Hessian. In distributed algorithms, estimating these quantities locally and combining them can introduce Hessian inversion bias. The paper studies this bias in distributed Newton methods and develops a correction based on shrinkage.

The central tool is an estimator for the resolvent of Gram matrices, an inverse-type matrix quantity relevant to the correction. The estimator is asymptotically unbiased, meaning its bias vanishes in the limiting regime considered by the analysis. The authors also characterize a finite-sample convergence rate in the isotropic case, providing a more specific guarantee under that condition.

They apply the estimator to correct Newton steps in distributed optimization and in methods based on randomized sketching. Analytical expressions expose the bias in naive averaging-based distributed Newton updates and allow comparison with the proposed approach. Experiments on real and synthetic datasets show substantial convergence improvements over standard baselines and recent proposals. The findings support correcting how inverse curvature is estimated as a useful route to faster optimization, while the unbiasedness guarantee is explicitly asymptotic.
icml-2023-optimal-shrinkage-for-distribu.tldr: A shrinkage-based, asymptotically unbiased matrix estimator corrects distributed Newton-step bias and improves convergence in experiments.

paragraphs: This paper systematically examines how prompting affects machine translation using GLM-130B as its testbed. It studies prompt templates, the selection of demonstration examples, and ways to use monolingual text. It also explores whether examples selected for one language, domain, or sentence-level setting can help in other translation settings.

The experiments show that both the number and quality of examples matter, and poor examples can degrade translation. Features such as semantic similarity have significant rank correlations with prompting performance, but none of the examined correlations is strong enough. This makes example selection more complicated than simply relying on one promising similarity signal.

The authors also find that zero-shot prompting can turn monolingual text into pseudo-parallel examples that may improve translation. Transferring prompt examples across settings can likewise produce gains, including the explored cross-lingual, cross-domain, and sentence-to-document transfers. Their output analysis identifies continuing problems with prompting. The study supplies evidence about practical prompt-design choices for the evaluated model, showing both opportunities to reuse data and the sensitivity of translation to demonstration quality.
icml-2023-prompting-large-language-model.tldr: A GLM-130B translation study shows that demonstration quality matters and that monolingual-derived examples and cross-setting transfer can improve prompting.

paragraphs: The paper asks whether quantum queries can accelerate the search for approximate stationary points of nonconvex functions. These are points where the gradient is sufficiently small, with accuracy controlled by ε. It studies two information-access settings: derivatives up to order p and stochastic gradients.

The authors extend known classical query lower bounds to quantum algorithms. For p-th order derivative access, the bound scales as ε raised to −(1+p)/p. With stochastic gradients, it scales as ε to −4, or ε to −3 under a mean-squared smoothness assumption. These lower bounds match the corresponding classical algorithmic results.

The proof shows that difficult classical instances retain their sequential structure even under quantum queries: information needed to find a stationary point must still be uncovered in sequence. Consequently, quantum access does not improve the worst-case query complexity in the studied settings, whether or not the stated stochastic smoothness assumption holds. The result identifies a concrete boundary on quantum optimization advantages tied to these derivative and gradient access models.
icml-2023-quantum-lower-bounds-for-findi.tldr: Matching quantum and classical query bounds rule out worst-case quantum speedups for nonconvex stationary-point search in the studied access models.

paragraphs: Urban prediction tasks such as traffic-flow and crime forecasting use graphs to represent relationships between regions over time. Their quality depends on how useful information is aggregated from those graphs. Noise and incomplete observations make it difficult to construct reliable region representations, motivating a method that adapts its own self-supervised training signals.

The proposed STAG model uses a learnable contrastive function to extract important signals from multiple views and guide adaptive graph augmentation. Its adversarial contrastive mechanism identifies hard samples to strengthen self-supervision. These components aim to improve both the ability to distinguish representations and their robustness to imperfect input information.

STAG also compares region representations across views, modeling their dependencies while preserving differences among relationship types. This allows the learning process to use shared information across views without discarding their distinct relational structure. Experiments on several benchmark datasets show superior performance across multiple spatial-temporal prediction tasks. The findings support adapting augmentation and sample difficulty to the data as useful components of graph-based urban representation learning.
icml-2023-spatial-temporal-graph-learnin.tldr: STAG adapts graph augmentation and hard-sample selection through adversarial contrastive learning to improve spatial-temporal prediction.

paragraphs: Aligning language models with instructions commonly uses reinforcement learning from human feedback, which adds complexity through reward and value networks. This paper explores a different use of feedback: converting it into revised instructions and then training the language model with a supervised objective. The approach requires no additional parameters beyond the original language model.

Hindsight Instruction Relabeling, or HIR, treats instruction following as a goal-reaching problem. Its two-stage procedure uses feedback to relabel instructions in hindsight and learns from the resulting instruction data. This design reuses much of the pretraining pipeline and illustrates a family of reward-free alignment methods built around relabeled instructions.

The authors evaluate HIR on twelve challenging BigBench reasoning tasks. It outperforms the evaluated baseline algorithms and performs comparably to, or better than, supervised fine-tuning. These findings support feedback-driven relabeling as a useful alternative training mechanism in the tested reasoning settings. The central idea is that feedback can improve instruction following by changing the supervised learning examples, allowing the original model to learn without additional reward or value networks.
icml-2023-the-wisdom-of-hindsight-makes-.tldr: HIR turns feedback into relabeled instructions for supervised language-model alignment without additional reward or value networks.

paragraphs: Image inpainting fills missing regions while keeping the result consistent with the visible parts of a reference image. Diffusion-based approaches often replace visible regions in generated images with reference pixels. The authors argue that this can leave the generated surroundings incoherent because the missing regions are not directly adjusted to fit that context.

CoPaint uses a Bayesian framework to modify visible and hidden regions jointly. Earlier Bayesian approaches can introduce mismatches through errors in approximating the posterior distribution. CoPaint instead uses an approximation whose errors are allowed to decrease to zero over the denoising steps, increasingly penalizing disagreement with the reference.

This connects two requirements of inpainting: the completed image should be coherent as a whole, and its revealed content should match the supplied image. Joint modification supports coherence, while the decreasing approximation error enforces reference agreement. Experiments show that CoPaint can outperform existing diffusion-based methods on both objective and subjective measures. The stated findings support controlling posterior approximation throughout denoising as a way to improve consistency in image completion.
icml-2023-towards-coherent-image-inpaint.tldr: CoPaint jointly adjusts visible and missing image regions while reducing posterior approximation error to produce coherent, reference-consistent inpainting.

paragraphs: Federated semi-supervised learning combines limited labeled data with abundant unlabeled data across clients. Existing approaches often assume that every class appears in the labeled set. FedoSSL addresses an open-world setting, where unlabeled examples can belong to previously unseen classes and their distribution differs across clients.

The paper identifies a resulting training imbalance. An unseen class present on several clients can receive stronger aggregation benefits than one present on only a single client. The authors call these locally unseen and globally unseen classes, respectively. Their uncertainty-aware suppressed loss is designed to reduce the unequal training effects between these groups.

FedoSSL also adds a calibration module to global aggregation to address potentially conflicting knowledge transfer between clients with inconsistent data distributions. The framework can be adapted to state-of-the-art federated learning methods, with experiments on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and CINIC-10 validating its use. The contribution is to make the distribution of unseen classes across clients an explicit training concern, addressing both unequal aggregation benefits and conflicts in transferred knowledge.
icml-2023-towards-unbiased-training-in-f.tldr: FedoSSL addresses uneven learning of unseen classes across federated clients through uncertainty-aware loss suppression and aggregation calibration.

paragraphs: Training graph neural networks can involve substantial unnecessary computation, while simply using more graph data does not resolve class imbalance. This paper investigates whether a smaller, informative training subset can support effective learning. Its theoretical starting point relates subset effectiveness to how closely the subset’s gradients match those of the full dataset.

Empirically, the authors observe that informative subsets change during training, a phenomenon they call dynamic data sparsity. They also find that pruning a contrastive model can remove valuable information, causing large losses on informative examples. These observations link which data are used with what information the sparse model retains.

Data Decantation, or DataDec, combines dynamic sparsity in the data and model within one framework. It uses sparse graph contrastive learning to identify informative training subsets as optimization proceeds. The authors evaluate its effectiveness on graph benchmarks and verify generalizability to image data. The contribution is an adaptive approach to reducing training data and computation while addressing representation quality, supported by both gradient-based reasoning and empirical observations about changing data usefulness.
icml-2023-when-sparsity-meets-contrastiv.tldr: DataDec dynamically selects informative data through sparse contrastive learning to address unnecessary computation and class-imbalanced representations.

paragraphs: A deployed model’s performance can change because several aspects of its data change at once. Possible factors include data quality, feature distributions, and the relationship between features and labels. This paper develops a way to assign portions of the performance difference between environments to shifts in the underlying data-generating mechanisms.

The authors formulate attribution as a cooperative game whose players are distributions. A group’s value is the performance change that would occur if only those distributions changed between environments. They derive an importance-weighting method to compute these values, allowing different combinations of shifts to be considered within the same framework.

Each distribution’s contribution is then quantified by its Shapley value, which allocates the total performance change using its contributions across combinations. This gives developers a structured explanation when multiple changes occur together. Synthetic, semi-synthetic, and real-world case studies demonstrate the method’s correctness and utility across a range of distribution shifts. The contribution is a formal attribution procedure that connects a measured performance difference to specific changes in the data-generating process.
icml-2023-why-did-the-model-fail-attribu.tldr: The method combines importance weighting and Shapley values to attribute model performance changes to individual distribution shifts.
